title: Paper Bridge: How Strong Is One Sheet?
description: One sheet of paper, two books, and a pile of coins. Test a flat bridge, then fold the same paper and test again — the difference will surprise you.

body.heading: A bridge made of almost nothing
paragraphs: Paper is floppy. Everyone knows that. But bridge engineers know a secret: shape can make a weak material strong. This model tests the same single sheet of paper two ways — flat, then folded — and counts exactly how much stronger shape makes it.

body.heading: Meet the parts
paragraphs: The span — the gap between the two books, the 'river' your bridge must cross. The deck — the paper itself, the road the load sits on. The supports — the two books, like the banks of a river. The load — coins added one at a time until the bridge gives up. The fold — the zigzag ridges you will add, called corrugation.

body.heading: You will need
paragraphs: Two books the same height, two sheets of paper from the same pad, a ruler, and a pile of coins (or washers) to use as test weights. A notebook to record your results like a real engineer.

paragraphs: Step 1 — Set the span. Place the books with a gap about as wide as your hand. Lay one flat sheet across them.
Step 2 — Test the flat bridge. Add coins one at a time, gently, in the middle. Count how many it holds before it sags into the gap. Write the number down.
Step 3 — Fold the second sheet. Fold it back and forth like a fan, making zigzag ridges from end to end. Lay it across the same gap, ridges running across the span.
Step 4 — Test the folded bridge. Add coins the same way, in the middle. Count again — most builders are amazed. Same paper, same span, far more strength.

body.heading: The science bit
paragraphs: A flat sheet bends easily because it is thin in the direction of the load. Folding zigzags makes the paper deep and ridged — and deep shapes resist bending far better than thin ones. The ridges spread the load out and hold each other up. It is exactly why cardboard boxes are made with a wavy layer inside, and why real steel bridge decks and roof panels are folded into ridges too.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Why did the SAME paper hold more coins after folding? What changed — the paper, or its shape?
2. Where can you find zigzag-folded material hiding in your house right now? (Hint: check a cardboard box's edge.)

takeaway: Folding paper into zigzag ridges makes the same sheet many times stronger — shape, not just material, decides how much a bridge can hold.
materials: Two sheets of paper from the same pad
Ruler (to set the same span every test)
supervision: A grown-up supervises testing and helps keep the span and coin placement the same for a fair test.
safetyNotes: Coins and washers are small parts — keep them away from children under 3, and wash hands after handling money.
Paper edges can give paper cuts — fold slowly and smooth ridges with the flat of your hand, not a fingertip run along the edge.
Build on a table so collapsing bridges drop coins onto the table, not the floor where bare feet walk.
screenFreeExtension: Bridge championship: challenge a family member — each of you folds one sheet any way you like, then test both bridges with coins and crown the strongest design in your engineering log.
